extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, navigators, and 17th-century scientific readers (mariners, meteorologists, experimental philosophers)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing and reporting observational natural-history and natural-philosophy (meteorology/dioptrics) accounts: systematic empirical observations, mechanistic hypotheses, and explanations that account for multiple phenomena and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic wind observations with geographic precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Record winds with specific latitudes, meridians, and compass points and note where patterns hold or change (e.g. 'near the coast of Africa... about the latitude of 28° north', 'limits of the trade winds... about the 30th degree of latitude').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed, location-referenced observational data: latitude bands, meridian references, compass bearings (N.E., S.E., W.S.W., etc.), distances (leagues), and how wind direction/strength varies with distance from land and as one sails (e.g. differences between African and American sides, coast vs open sea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report seasonal and temporal variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe how the season of the year affects winds and monsoons (e.g. 'the season of the year has some small effect', 'monsoons blow from October to April... and from April to October the opposite').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include timing (months, seasons) for changes in prevailing winds and monsoons, note periods when winds shift or are more tempestuous (e.g. 'breaking up of the monsoons'), and relate voyage timing to favourable/unfavourable wind seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document anomalies and local phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Note and describe exceptions to general rules such as calms, tornadoes, 'the Rains' (perpetual calms with thunder and lightning), and tempestuous periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report frequency, local names, and effects on navigation (e.g. 'frequent calms, violent sudden gusts called tornadoes', 'this part of the sea the Rains'), and indicate where and when such anomalies occur so hypotheses must account for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must proceed from a permanent unintermitting cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a current is perpetual and fixed in its course, 'it is necessary that it proceed from a permanent unintermitting cause.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed causes for persistent phenomena should be long-lasting and not ad hoc; they must be capable of producing steady, globe-spanning effects and be robust to known counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement with known properties and laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations should be 'agreeable to the known properties of the elements of air and water, and the laws of the motion of fluid bodies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base hypotheses on established physical principles (properties of air/water, statics, fluid motion); avoid mechanisms inconsistent with known behavior of fluids or with other empirical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the full set of observed phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory solution must account for multiple listed phenomena (Halley's six problems): why easterly winds predominate between 30° N and S; why trade winds extend to about 30°; why a constant south-westerly wind exists near Guinea; why the northern Indian Ocean has semi-annual monsoons while its southern part does not; why trade-winds incline north/south of east; and why the Chinese seas show a greater inclination from the east to the north.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly demonstrate how the hypothesis explains each enumerated empirical fact and the relations among them rather than addressing only one aspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for continental and surface effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider 'the nature of the soil, and the position of the high mountains' as principal causes of local variations in wind patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include how land heating/cooling, mountain ranges, soil/ground properties (reflection/retention of heat), and proximity to coasts modify general atmospheric circulation and produce regional deviations (e.g. westerly near Guinea due to hot inland areas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use circulation and vertical structure in explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoke vertical circulation and upper-air return flows to explain surface wind patterns (e.g. ascent of warmed air, upper currents moving opposite to lower trades).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how lower-level winds pair with compensating upper-level flows, and use this circulation to make sense of rapid reversals and monsoon behavior; connect vertical motions to precipitation and 'Rains' where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative and practical reporting in natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: In observational-natural-history reports (e.g. locusts), give quantitative measures, life-cycle timing, observed counts/weights, and outcomes of interventions (e.g. 'we took of them 180 quintals, being 9 tons').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record amounts, sizes, dates, life stages, and practical control measures and their effectiveness; note uncertainties (e.g. inability to determine particular species) and recommend timely interventions when supported by data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanistic explanation tied to observation (solar heating example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose mechanisms that link observed phenomena to physical drivers (e.g. sunbeams heating air/water leading to general easterly winds and a circulation that drives trade-winds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show causal chain from driver (solar heating) through intermediate physical effects (rarefaction/expansion, pressure tendencies, advection by sun's westward apparent motion) to observed outcomes; demonstrate consistency with seasonal and geographic variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dioptric/optical explanations grounded in instrument geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain optical phenomena (e.g. why four convex-glasses show objects erect) by precise geometric placement: distances relative to foci and the eye's position ('the eye... is placed in the focus of this nearest eye-glass').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break complex optical instruments into subcomponents, show how each lens and the eye's placement affect image inversion/erection, and justify claims by reasoning about focal positions and what each lens contributes to the species seen by the eye.
